chunks.title: Period Pain
chunks.text:
Causes of period pain
Period pain happens when your womb tightens during your period. It's often a normal part
of the menstrual cycle. Sometimes painful periods can be caused by a condition such as:
womb-like tissue growing in other places (endometriosis (Link:
www.nhs.uk/conditions/endometriosis/) and adenomyosis (Link:
www.nhs.uk/conditions/adenomyosis/))
growths in and around the womb (fibroids (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/fibroids/))
an infection of the womb, fallopian tubes and ovaries (pelvic inflammatory disease (Link:
www.nhs.uk/conditions/pelvic-inflammatory-disease-pid/))
An intrauterine device (IUD) (Link: www.nhs.uk/contraception/methods-of-contraception/iudcoil/) can also cause period pain, particularly during the first 3 to 6 months after it's put in. your pelvic pain or period pain is severe or worse than usual, and painkillers
have not helped
You can call 111 or get help from 111 online (Link: https://111.nhs.uk/triage/checkyour-symptoms).

chunks.title: Period Pain
chunks.text:
Period pain
It's common to have pain or discomfort before or during your period. There are things you
can do to help ease the pain. Symptoms of period pain
Period pain usually happens to women and girls around the start of their period. It can affect
anyone who has periods. You may have period pain if:
you have pain in your tummy at the start of your period, or just before your period
you have painful cramps in your tummy that spread to your back and thighs
you have a sharp pain or a dull ache in your tummy
Period pain usually lasts for up to 3 days and can affect your daily activities. How you can ease period pain
There are some things you can do to help ease period pain. Cutting down on alcohol (Link: www.nhs.uk/live-well/alcohol-advice/) and not
smoking (Link: www.nhs.uk/live-well/quit-smoking/) may also help ease period pain.

Treatments for period pain
If you have severe period pain, a GP may recommend:
anti-inflammatory medicines like naproxen (Link: www.nhs.uk/medicines/naproxen/),
flurbiprofen or mefenamic acid
a TENS machine (Link: www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/transcutaneous-electrical-nervestimulation-tens/) – a small device that uses mild electrical impulses to reduce pain
contraception (Link: www.nhs.uk/contraception/) like the pill, implant or injection – these
thin the womb lining, making your period lighter and easing the pain
The GP may refer you to a specialist (gynaecologist) if your period pain does not get better or
they think you may have a condition, like fibroids, causing your pain. You might need tests, such as an ultrasound scan (Link: www.nhs.uk/tests-andtreatments/ultrasound-scan/), to find out what's causing your period pain. If a condition is
found, treating it will help. For example, if you have fibroids, you may be given medicine to shrink them or have surgery
to remove them. If you have pelvic inflammatory disease, you'll usually need antibiotics.
